source_text: ἀνθρωπίνων ἠθῶν ὑποτύπωσιν, ζῶά τε πολλὰ τῶν ἀλόγων, καὶ μὴν καὶ πτηνῶν καὶ ἐνύδρων γένη παρενεγκὼν, κατὰ μυρίους ἡμᾶς ὀνίνησι τρόπους. Καὶ μή τι θαυμάσῃς, ὅπου καὶ αὐτοῖς ἔσθ' ὅτε παρεικάζει φυτοῖς, ἀπὸ τῆς ἑκάστου ποιότητος φυσικῆς. κατασημαίνων ἀστείως τὰ ἐφ' ἑκάστῳ τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς. Ἔφη γάρ που Θεὸς διὰ φωνῆς Ἡσαΐου, τῶν εἰς Χριστὸν διὰ πίστεως ἀνατεθαλκότων εἰς ζωὴν τὰς εὐοσμίας ὑποδηλῶν, δῆλον δὲ ὅτι τὰς πνευματικὰς, καὶ μὴν καὶ ὑψώματα τὰ εἰς ἀρετήν· «Καὶ ποιήσω ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ὕδωρ ζῶν, καὶ ἐν γῇ ἀνύδρῳ ποταμοὺς, καὶ θήσω εἰς τὴν ἄνυδρον γῆν, κέδρον, καὶ πύξον, καὶ μυρσίνην, καὶ κυπάρισσον, καὶ λεύκην.» Καὶ πάλιν· «Καὶ ἔσται,» φησὶν, «ἀντὶ τῆς στοιβῆς, ἀναβήσεται κυπάρισσος· ἀντὶ δὲ κονύζης, ἀναβήσεται μυρσίνη·» στοιβὴν, οἶμαί που, καὶ κόνυζαν, τὰς ἀνημέρους ἔτι ψυχὰς, καὶ ἐν εἴδει τῆς ἀγρίας ἀκάνθης ἐκφαινομένας παρά γε τοῖς τῆς θεότητος ὀφθαλμοῖς, ὀνομάζων εὐφυῶς. Ἀλλὰ καὶ λίθοις ἔσθ' ὅτε τὸ σεπτὸν τῶν ἁγίων παρεικάζεται στίφος· «Λίθοι γὰρ ἅγιοι κυλίονται ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.» Καὶ μὴν καὶ ζύμῃ προσεοικέναι καὶ κόκκῳ σινάπεως τὴν τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλείαν ἔφασκεν ὁ Σωτήρ. Ἐκ πολλῶν οὖν ἄρα καὶ ἐναργεστάτων παραδειγμάτων καταδηλοῦν ἔθος τῇ θεοπνεύστῳ Γραφῇ τὰ ἀνθρώπινα. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Σύμφημι. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἄθρει δὴ οὖν ὅτι μυρία μὲν ὅσα κτηνῶν εἴδη, καὶ μὴν τὰ πτηνῶν καὶ τὰ νηκτῶν παρενεγκοῦσα χρησίμως, τὰ μὲν, ὡς ἀκάθαρτα καταμιαίνει παντελῶς, τὰ δὲ αὖ προσίεταί τε καὶ ἀπαλλάττει διαβολῆς, ἵν' εἰδεῖεν ὀρθῶς οἱ Θεῷ λατρεύοντες, τίνα μὲν δρῶντες, οὐκ εἰσδεχθεῖεν ἄν· τίνων δὲ νουνεχῶς ἀπεσχημένοι, μώμου μὲν ἔσονται μακρὰν, λαμπροὶ δ' ἂν εἶεν καὶ ἀξιόληπτοι, καὶ ψήφῳ τῇ ἄνωθεν τετιμημένοι. Ἔχει δὲ οὕτως ἡμῖν ὁ ἐπὶ τῷδε νόμος· «Καὶ ἐλάλησε Κύριος πρὸς Μωσῆν καὶ Ἀαρὼν, λέγων· Λαλήσατε τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ, λέγοντες· Ταῦτα τὰ κτήνη, ἃ φάγεσθε ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν κτηνῶν τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, πᾶν κτῆνος διχηλοῦν ὁπλὴν, καὶ ὀνυχιστῆρας ὀνυχίζον δύο χηλῶν, καὶ ἀνάγον μηρυκισμὸν ἐν τοῖς κτήνεσι, ταῦτα φάγεσθε· πλὴν ἀπὸ τούτων οὐ φάγεσθε, ἀπὸ τῶν ἀναγόντων μηρυκισμὸν, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν διχηλούντων τὰς ὁπλὰς, καὶ ὀνυχιζόντων ὀνυχιστῆρας· τὸν κάμηλον, ὅτι ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν, ὁπλὴν δὲ οὐ διχηλεῖ, ἀκάθαρτον τοῦτο ὑμῖν, καὶ τὸν δασύποδα, ὅτι ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν καὶ ὁπλὴν οὐ διχηλεῖ, ἀκάθαρτον τοῦτο ὑμῖν, καὶ τὸν χοιρογρύλλιον, ὅτι ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν, καὶ ὁπλὴν οὐ διχηλεῖ, ἀκάθαρτον τοῦτο ὑμῖν, καὶ τὸν ὗν, ὅτι διχηλεῖ ὁπλὴν, τοῦτο καὶ ὀνυχίζει ὄνυχας ὁπλῆς, καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ ἀνάγει μηρυκισμὸν, ἀκάθαρτον τοῦτο ὑμῖν. Ἀπὸ τῶν κρεῶν αὐτῶν οὐ φάγεσθε, καὶ τῶν θνησιμαίων αὐτῶν οὐ φάγεσθε, ἀκάθαρτα ταῦτα ὑμῖν.» Ἐναργέστατα μὲν οὖν ὁ Χριστὸς, «Οὐ τὸ εἰσερχόμενον εἰς τὸ στόμα,» φησὶ, «κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον.» Εἴρηται δέ που καὶ πρὸς τὸν θεσπέσιον Πέτρον, τῆς σινδόνος ἄνωθεν καθιεμένης τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς, ἐν ᾗ πάντα γέγραπται τὰ
pass_a_gloss: [Cyril, continuing the law’s subject] …for a sketch of human habits, having brought in many of the irrational animals, and also kinds of winged and water creatures, benefits us in countless ways. And do not wonder, since sometimes it likens even to plants themselves, from the natural quality of each, signifying elegantly the things in each of our [affairs]. For God said somewhere through Isaiah’s voice, hinting at the fragrances, clearly spiritual, of those who toward Christ through faith have blossomed again into life, and also the heights toward virtue: And I will make in the desert living water, and in waterless land rivers, and I will set in the waterless land cedar, box, myrtle, cypress, white poplar. And again: And it shall be instead of the brushwood/scrub a cypress will go up; instead of fleabane a myrtle will go up; scrub and fleabane, I think, naming aptly the souls still untamed, appearing in the form of the wild thorn in the eyes of the Godhead. But also to stones sometimes the venerable band of the saints is likened: For holy stones are rolled upon the earth. And indeed the Savior said the kingdom of the heavens resembles leaven and a grain of mustard. From many and most vivid examples therefore it is the custom of the God-inspired Scripture to make plain human things. [Palladius] I agree. [Cyril] Look, then, that [Scripture, fem. participle ] bringing forward usefully countless kinds of cattle, and those of birds and swimmers, some as unclean it defiles entirely, others it admits and frees from slander/reproach, so that those serving God may know rightly by doing what they would not be received, and by abstaining sensibly from what they will be far from blame, and would be bright, worthy of acceptance, honored by the vote from above. The law on this is thus: And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: These are the beasts which you will eat from all the beasts on the earth: every beast dividing the hoof and clawing claws of two hooves, and bringing up the cud among the beasts, these you will eat; except of these you will not eat, of those bringing up the cud and of those dividing the hoofs and clawing claws: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you; and the hare, because it brings up the cud and does not divide the hoof, unclean to you; and the rock badger, because it brings up the cud and does not divide the hoof, unclean to you; and the pig, because it divides the hoof, and this claws the claws of the hoof, and this does not bring up the cud, unclean to you. Of their meat you will not eat, and of their carcasses you will not eat; these are unclean to you. Most plainly Christ: Not what enters into the mouth makes common the man. pass_b_english: Cyril: …brings in many irrational animals, and kinds of birds and water creatures as well, to sketch human characters, and so benefits us in countless ways. And do not be surprised at this, since at times it likens us even to plants, using the natural quality of each to mark out neatly what belongs to each of us. For God said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, hinting at the fragrance of those who through faith in Christ have blossomed anew into life (a spiritual fragrance, clearly), and at the heights they reach in virtue: ‘And I will make living water in the desert, and rivers in a waterless land’ (Isaiah 43:19–20), ‘and I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box tree, the myrtle, the cypress and the white poplar.’ (Isaiah 41:19) And again: ‘And it shall be,’ he says, ‘that instead of the scrub a cypress shall come up, and instead of the fleabane a myrtle shall come up.’ (Isaiah 55:13) By scrub and fleabane, I think, he aptly names souls still untamed, which appear in the eyes of the Godhead like wild thorn. And at times the venerable company of the saints is also likened to stones: ‘For holy stones are rolling on the earth.’ (Zechariah 9:16) And the Savior, too, said that the kingdom of heaven is like leaven and like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–33). So it is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to make human things plain through many very vivid examples.

Cyril: Observe, then, that Scripture, bringing forward to good purpose countless kinds of beasts, and of birds and swimming creatures too, brands some as unclean and wholly defiled, and accepts others again and clears them of reproach, so that those who serve God may rightly know what conduct would keep them from being accepted, and by wisely abstaining from what they will be far from blame and will shine, worthy of acceptance and honored by the verdict from above. The law on this matter runs as follows: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say: These are the animals that you shall eat out of all the animals on the earth. Every animal that parts the hoof and is cloven-footed with two claws, and brings up the cud, among the animals, these you shall eat. But of these you shall not eat, of those that bring up the cud and of those that part the hoof and are cloven-footed: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the hare, because it brings up the cud and does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the rock badger, because it brings up the cud and does not part the hoof; it is unclean to you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed, but does not bring up the cud; it is unclean to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall not eat of their carcasses; they are unclean to you.’ (Leviticus 11:1–8) Now Christ says most plainly: ‘It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person.’ (Matthew 15:11) And somewhere it was also said to the inspired Peter, when the sheet was let down from above by its four corners (Acts 10:11–12), in which, it is written, were all the…

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

PG 68.916. Opens mid-sentence: §15 ends ‘Θέα δὴ οὖν ὅπως αἰνιγματωδῶς ὁ νόμος εἰς’ and the law (masc. παρενεγκών) is the subject of ὀνίνησι here; the English splits as ‘See, then, how the law, speaking in riddles,…’ / ‘…brings in … and so benefits us’. The first Isaiah quotation is a conflation: ‘I will make in the desert … in a waterless land rivers’ matches Isaiah 43:19 LXX (ποιήσω ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ὁδὸν καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ ποταμούς), where Cyril has ‘living water’ for ‘a way’, the ‘water’ coming from 43:20 LXX (ἔδωκα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ὕδωρ καὶ ποταμοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ), so cited 43:19–20; the tree list matches Isaiah 41:19 LXX exactly (θήσω εἰς τὴν ἄνυδρον γῆν κέδρον καὶ πύξον καὶ μυρσίνην καὶ κυπάρισσον καὶ λεύκην). Both are cited beside their clauses. Isaiah 55:13 LXX quoted (στοιβή ‘brushwood, thorny scrub’; κόνυζα ‘fleabane’, a rank-smelling weed; English Bibles from the Hebrew have ‘thorn’ and ‘brier’). Zechariah 9:16 LXX (λίθοι ἅγιοι κυλίονται ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς αὐτοῦ; Cyril drops αὐτοῦ); the Hebrew differs (‘jewels of a crown’). Matthew 13:31–33 (mustard seed and leaven; Luke 13:18–21 is parallel). Leviticus 11:1–8 LXX quoted with Cyril’s variants: his text has ‘you shall not eat of their carcasses’ where the LXX has ‘you shall not touch’ (οὐχ ἅψεσθε); rendered as he has it. The hare stands before the rock badger, as in the LXX order; the Hebrew and English Bibles put the rock badger first (Leviticus 11:5) and the hare second (11:6). ὀνυχιστῆρας ὀνυχίζον δύο χηλῶν rendered ‘is cloven-footed with two claws’; μηρυκισμὸν ἀνάγει kept literal as ‘brings up the cud’ because §18’s reading depends on bringing food up from the belly. Matthew 15:11 quoted in short form (NA: οὐ τὸ εἰσερχόμενον εἰς τὸ στόμα κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον). Acts 10:11–12 summarised (the sheet by four corners); quotation of Acts 10:13 follows in §17. ἐν ᾗ πάντα γέγραπται: γέγραπται likely ‘it is written’ (in Acts) rather than ‘depicted’; taken so. Scripture (feminine participle παρενεγκοῦσα) is the subject of the third Cyril turn. θεόπνευστος echoes 2 Timothy 3:16 as a word only; uncited. ‘The Godhead’ for ἡ θεότης.
Isaiah citation moved outside the quotation and widened to 43:19–20 (ὕδωρ is from 43:20 LXX)
removed added 'must' in the abstaining clause; future/optative kept (ἔσονται ... εἶεν)
